title: Nandaka's full moon
hookLine: an elder teaches the nuns; they are satisfied like the full moon

lines: FIVE HUNDRED NUNS ASK TO BE TAUGHT.
cards: Mahapajapati Gotami comes to the Buddha again, this time with five hundred nuns, asking him to teach them. In the hundred and forty-sixth discourse, the senior monks have been taking turns teaching the nuns.

It's the turn of an elder named Nandaka, and he doesn't want to go. The discourse doesn't say why. The Buddha asks Ananda whose turn it is, hears the answer, and turns to Nandaka himself: teach the nuns, Nandaka.
Give them a talk on the teaching. So Nandaka goes.

teach.b: He teaches by asking. Sisters, is the eye permanent or impermanent? Impermanent, venerable sir.
And what's impermanent, is it pain or ease? Pain, venerable sir. Is it fit to be called mine, me, my self?
No, venerable sir. Through all six senses, their objects, and their kinds of knowing. Then three pictures.
An oil lamp is burning: the oil, the wick and the flame all change. Would anyone say its light stays the same forever? A great tree: its roots, trunk, branches and leaves all change.

teach.h: A LAMP, A TREE, A SHARP KNIFE
teach.b: And a skilled butcher with a sharp knife, separating the hide from the flesh without cutting either: that's wisdom, slicing cleanly through what binds the mind. The nuns are pleased.
But the Buddha sees they're glad, not yet fulfilled. Teach them again tomorrow, Nandaka, the same way. So he does.
Then the Buddha uses the moon.
On the fourteenth night, nobody looking up doubts it: the moon isn't full yet. That was the nuns after the first talk. On the fifteenth, nobody doubts either: the moon is full.
That's the nuns after the second. The text says the least of the five hundred had entered the stream.
Look back at the week: many names for a bowl, a stranger in a potter's shed, the truths expounded, a robe made by hand, a dying giver, Punna going west.
And now a reluctant teacher, sent back a second time, until the moon was full.

how: The monastic rules ask the nuns' community to receive instruction (ovada) from the monks every half-month, and MN 146 shows one such teaching, given by questions and answers.

o: a new moon, dark and hidden from view
a monk who teaches the nuns their rules
full, like the moon on the fifteenth night

games.q: Nandaka's full moon: tap the pairs.
p: the elder whose turn it was to teach
oil, wick and flame all change

s: Nandaka is eager to teach the nuns
he doesn't want to go; the Buddha himself asks him to teach.
after the first talk, the nuns are glad but not yet fulfilled
the Buddha sends Nandaka back to teach them again the next day.
Nandaka teaches mostly by asking the nuns questions
is the eye permanent or impermanent? is it fit to be called mine?

games.q: you're the Buddha. the nuns are pleased with Nandaka's talk, but you see they aren't yet fulfilled. what do you do?
o: send Nandaka back to teach the same way tomorrow.
tell the nuns to study on their own.
games.why: Nandaka teaches again in the same way, and the nuns become like the moon on the fifteenth: full.

practice: Think of one small thing you know well, how to make rice, how to calm down before a call, one line from this path, and picture someone who'd benefit.
Picture teaching it the way Nandaka did: asking, not lecturing, and willing to say it again if it hasn't landed. Then let the picture go, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Punna. Full: a reluctant elder named Nandaka teaches the nuns twice, and they go from nearly full, like the fourteenth night, to full, like the fifteenth. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali punna: full. the moon of the fifteenth is full, and so are the nuns after the second talk.

carryVoice: Your line: the moon is full. Sometimes a teaching needs a second night to land. A week done; see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 146, Nandakovada Sutta (advice from Nandaka)
